title: Intercultural Competence

slides.title: One DSD People, Access and Culture
slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Intercultural Competence

Understanding cultural perspectives and how everyday choices shape DSD services and workplace opportunity.

Self-directed Foundation learning for all staff
slides.narration:
A service explanation, an onboarding conversation, or a meeting invitation can seem ordinary. Each also carries assumptions about how people understand information, express concerns, and participate. When those assumptions do not fit, someone may lose the opportunity to explain what matters. Repeated across a process, that small gap can become a persistent barrier.

This course helps you notice that connection and choose a more thoughtful response. You will examine service, workplace, and community situations. Read at your own pace, consider the questions, and use the answer explanations to examine your reasoning. The aim is to understand cultural meaning without predicting anyone from their identity. You do not need to disclose a personal experience or an actual case.

slides.title: Your learning
slides.text:
Your learning

Consider each practice situation privately. You do not need to disclose personal, employee, or case information.

Choose a response, read its explanation, and reconsider what you know and what remains uncertain.

Look beyond intent: whose participation could the action change, especially if it becomes routine?
slides.narration:
You can work through these examples on your own. When a question appears, pause long enough to form your own answer before reading further. The explanation may confirm part of your thinking and also reveal an effect you had not considered. That is a useful part of learning, not a judgment about your character.

Keep three questions in mind: What did the person actually do? What might the response make possible or more difficult? What could happen if the same response became routine? An interruption can reduce one person's voice; repeated interruptions can influence whose ideas shape decisions. Cultural context may help you ask better questions, but it does not settle why an individual acted. No one needs to represent an entire community.

slides.title: Different ways of seeing
slides.text:
Different ways of seeing

A service discussion accepts comments only during the meeting. Someone needs more time or another way to contribute.

Their knowledge may be missed. Repeating that format can narrow whose experience shapes services.

Before reading on, choose one change and explain what you would need to check with participants.
slides.narration:
Imagine that you are preparing a discussion about a service change. The invitation says that comments will be taken during a short live meeting. What might happen to someone who needs time to consider the material, communication support, or a different way to respond? Form an answer before continuing.

The format may work well for some people. It becomes a concern when it is the only route and relevant perspectives cannot reach the discussion. A written option, accessible preparation material, or another conversation could help, but you would still ask participants what works for them. A culture brief can prepare that question. The same pattern can affect a new employee whose thoughtful written contributions are overlooked in fast meetings.

slides.title: Belonging and group identity
slides.text:
Belonging and group identity

Unwritten expectations can leave a newcomer unsure how to contribute. Their silence may then be mistaken for lack of interest.

If that judgment shapes later assignments, an onboarding gap can become an opportunity gap.

Make expectations clear and ask what would help. What evidence would change your first interpretation?
slides.narration:
Belonging includes knowing how to enter a conversation and having a fair opportunity to contribute. A new employee may understand the subject but not know how this team asks questions or influences decisions. If the team leaves those expectations unexplained, silence may be interpreted as disengagement. That interpretation can then affect feedback and development assignments.

Consider what would change your first impression. Relevant written work, a direct conversation, or a review of meeting conditions could clarify what is happening. Explain expectations and invite the employee's perspective without assigning a cultural explanation. A person using services can face a similar gap when unfamiliar language and meeting routines are mistaken for lack of interest. The conditions of participation deserve attention before the person is judged.

slides.title: Practice: a service explanation
slides.text:
Practice: a service explanation

A person sets a translated renewal notice aside. Their family offers to answer every question. What would best support a respectful discussion?

A. Rely on the family’s answers because the notice was translated.

B. Ask the person how they prefer to review the steps and whom they want involved.

C. Record that the person is uninterested in the renewal.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Rely on the family’s answers because the notice was translated.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Ask the person how they prefer to review the steps and whom they want involved.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Record that the person is uninterested in the renewal.

slides.narration:

slides.title: Intention and impact
slides.text:
Intention and impact

A staff member answers for a person to be helpful. The person loses the chance to explain their priorities.

If this becomes routine, plans may reflect other people’s assumptions rather than the person’s wishes.

Return the conversation to the person and ask about chosen support. What would you change next time?
slides.narration:
The intention may be caring, and the effect may still need attention. Answering for someone can remove their chance to describe what matters. If those answers guide a plan, the omission becomes more than a moment in conversation: it may shape the options the person receives. Repeating the approach can make someone else's interpretation the usual source of information.

A useful response is to acknowledge the interruption, return the question to the person, and ask whom they want involved. Their answer may include family or another supporter; restoring voice does not mean excluding chosen support. Internally, a supervisor who finishes an employee's idea may also affect whose knowledge receives credit. Repair the exchange, then examine the routine that made it easy to repeat.

slides.title: Understanding another perspective
slides.text:
Understanding another perspective

A person’s meaning of independence may include close family relationships. Staff may assume it means doing everything alone.

That assumption can narrow the support options discussed and become embedded in planning routines.

Ask what the person wants and who they want involved. A brief prepares questions; the person explains their meaning.
slides.narration:
Before deciding how to respond, consider what the person means. Independence might mean controlling one's choices while staying closely connected with family or community. If staff equate independence with doing everything alone, they may overlook support that matters to the person. Used repeatedly in forms or planning conversations, that expectation can narrow what is recognized as a successful outcome.

Ask what the person wants to do and which relationships they want to maintain. A culture brief can prompt thoughtful questions about family and support, but it cannot answer for this individual. In a development conversation, an employee may also define meaningful growth differently from the usual promotion route. Understanding the meaning creates a stronger basis for offering real choices.

slides.title: The Golden Rule
slides.text:
The Golden Rule

The Golden Rule encourages the care and respect we would want to receive.

Using only our preferred approach may still make information or feedback harder for another person to use.

Ask what works for them. Which of your own preferences could become an unnecessary requirement?
slides.narration:
The care behind the Golden Rule is valuable. Its limitation appears when our own preference becomes the only approach we offer. You may appreciate immediate verbal feedback, while another person needs written information and time to prepare questions. Giving everyone your preferred version may be equal in delivery but unequal in usability.

Consider one preference of your own that could become a requirement without you noticing. Perhaps it concerns pace, meeting participation, or how someone demonstrates understanding. Ask the person what would help rather than infer a preference from identity. In onboarding and service explanations, flexible communication can make the information more usable. If the same barrier appears repeatedly, review the standard format as well as the individual conversation.

slides.title: The Platinum Rule
slides.text:
The Platinum Rule

The Platinum Rule asks us to learn how another person wishes to be treated.

Adjust an explanation, meeting format, or feedback approach when appropriate; explain any limits clearly.

Check whether the change helped. A repeated adjustment may reveal a default that needs review.
slides.narration:
Learning another person's preference helps us respond to the actual situation. It does not mean guessing from a community description or promising every requested change. Ask what would support participation, consider what is possible within your role, and explain limits clearly. Then ask whether the response was useful.

An adjustment may remove an immediate barrier while revealing a wider issue. If many people need the same clarification, the notice itself may need attention. If new employees repeatedly need unwritten expectations explained, onboarding may need a clearer introduction. Do not assume that one adjustment has solved everything. Listening after the change helps distinguish a helpful intention from an improvement the person can actually use.

slides.title: Intercultural competence
slides.text:
Intercultural competence

Intercultural competence connects understanding cultural meaning with an appropriate response.

Ask whose expectations shape a service or workplace routine and how that routine affects participation.

Try an adjustment supported by what you learn. What would show that it helped rather than merely changed the interaction? This course does not assess anyone’s intercultural development.
slides.narration:
Intercultural competence involves curiosity, understanding, and action. Cultural knowledge can help you recognize that your first interpretation is not the only possible one. The next step is to ask about the person's meaning and consider an appropriate response. Competence is not memorizing how members of a group supposedly behave.

Across recruitment, onboarding, supervision, development, and retention, familiar expectations can influence whose contribution becomes visible. Service decisions can carry similar expectations about family, communication, and participation. Ask how the routine works for those affected and whether an adjustment improves a real opportunity. Community listening and culture briefs inform the inquiry in different ways. A brief offers context; the person's response helps you examine this particular experience. You can use these questions to learn, but this course cannot determine anyone’s intercultural development assessment result.

C. Use the learning discussion to identify the employee’s IDI orientation.

slides.title: Intercultural Development Continuum
slides.text:
Intercultural Development Continuum

The continuum describes Denial, Polarization, Minimization, Acceptance, and Adaptation as orientations toward cultural difference.

Use it to examine approaches and what they may overlook, not to label people.

A course answer or helpful action cannot establish anyone’s IDI result.
slides.narration:
The continuum offers a framework for thinking about approaches to cultural difference. As you read the next examples, examine what an approach makes visible and what it leaves out. That is different from deciding where a colleague or service recipient sits on the continuum.

One action can have several explanations. An inaccessible notice may reveal a design gap; it does not by itself reveal its author's developmental orientation. An adjustment may help someone participate; it does not establish an IDI result. An unsupported label may influence later feedback or development opportunities. If retained as a routine judgment, it can replace evidence about the work with an unverified assessment. The course invites you to examine reasoning and consequences in practice situations. Keep the evidence about the interaction separate from a claim about the person. That distinction allows serious discussion of barriers without turning the framework into a ranking tool.

slides.title: Denial
slides.text:
Denial

Denial involves limited attention to cultural difference or difficulty recognizing its relevance.

An unfamiliar perspective may never enter a service or onboarding discussion. Repeated omissions can shape what the system notices.

Whose experience could widen the question? Identify a way to learn without labeling anyone.
slides.narration:
Consider an orientation that assumes everyone understands the same workplace terms. Employees who do not know those terms may struggle to ask questions. If their difficulty remains unnoticed, the team may continue judging readiness without examining the information gap. A service discussion can make a similar assumption about program language.

Within the continuum, Denial concerns limited attention to cultural difference. The useful question here is what the approach leaves unseen, not what label should be assigned to a person. A brief can introduce context unfamiliar to staff, while direct listening can reveal a specific need the brief could not predict. Think about one perspective that might change the question and one respectful way to hear it.

slides.title: Polarization
slides.text:
Polarization

Polarization frames difference through “us and them.” Defense favors one’s own group; Reversal devalues it in favor of another.

Dismissing knowledge by group can silence concerns and narrow the evidence used in decisions.

What is the specific concern, and what could each perspective help explain?
slides.narration:
In this example, a service team dismisses community concerns because it believes outsiders do not understand the program. A different response dismisses all staff knowledge as irrelevant. Both replace examination of the issue with a judgment about a group. That can silence information needed to understand the service's effects.

If this becomes routine, the same voices may be excluded whenever decisions are made. Ask what the particular concern is, what evidence supports it, and what each perspective contributes. Understanding does not require agreement with every proposal. In workplace disagreements, the same approach helps keep an employee's contribution visible rather than treating it as the view of an opposing group. Examine the argument and its effects without assigning anyone an orientation.

slides.title: Minimization
slides.text:
Minimization

Minimization emphasizes common needs while overlooking differences that affect participation.

The same notice or onboarding package may be unusable for some people. Reusing it can preserve the access gap.

What difference matters to this shared goal, and how could the requirement become usable?
slides.narration:
Shared goals and common humanity matter. They do not tell us whether everyone can use the same approach. A renewal notice or onboarding package may reach everyone and still be difficult for some people to understand, navigate, or act on. Saying that everyone received it leaves that question unanswered.

Within the continuum, Minimization draws attention to the limits of stopping at common needs. Ask what meaningful difference the routine may overlook. Community feedback and employee experience can clarify language, format, timing, or background information. If the same format is repeatedly treated as sufficient, those barriers can remain part of the process. Consider an adjustment that preserves the purpose while making participation more usable, then check its effect.

slides.title: Acceptance
slides.text:
Acceptance

Acceptance recognizes meaningful cultural differences alongside common ground.

Explore what independence, support, or professional growth means to the person before offering options.

Understanding improves the decision’s basis; leaving the routine unchanged may still leave a barrier. What response deserves consideration?
slides.narration:
Acceptance makes room to understand a cultural perspective on its own terms. A person may describe independence through relationships and chosen support. An employee may value professional growth that does not follow the usual advancement path. Listening carefully helps you understand what is being sought before deciding what can be offered.

There is still work to do after understanding. If the available options reflect only the team's familiar definition, the person may remain constrained. Ask whether a routine, criterion, or format needs consideration within the responsible role. You do not need to agree with every request to examine it fairly. Understanding creates a stronger basis for a response; it does not by itself demonstrate that the person's opportunity has changed.

slides.title: Adaptation
slides.text:
Adaptation

Adaptation involves considering another cultural perspective and adjusting behavior appropriately.

Change an explanation, meeting approach, or feedback conversation in response to what you learn.

Ask what improved and what remains difficult. If the barrier recurs, consider whether the routine also needs attention.
slides.narration:
Adaptation carries understanding into action. A team might revise a community discussion because people say the original format prevents useful participation. A supervisor might adjust a feedback conversation after learning how an employee can best consider the information. The change should respond to what was learned, rather than to a prediction about identity.

Ask whether the adjustment helped and what remains difficult. If people still cannot contribute, the invitation, timing, or decision process may need further attention. A recurring barrier may call for review beyond one conversation. You can consider the change and its limits without claiming it has eliminated an inequity. A single helpful action also does not establish anyone's intercultural orientation.

slides.title: Practice: a translated notice
slides.text:
Practice: a translated notice

A person sets a translated renewal notice aside and says they have no questions.

Assuming understanding may leave next steps unclear; repeated assumptions can make the notice an access barrier.

Choose an open question about format or next steps. What could the answer establish that the action alone cannot?
slides.narration:
Pause before interpreting the action. Setting a notice aside might mean that the person understands it, prefers another format, wants time, or has another reason entirely. What open question would help you learn? Form a response before reading further.

You might ask how the person would like to review the next steps and whether anything needs clarification. Their answer gives you information that the observed action does not. If staff routinely equate translation with understanding, people who need another explanation may lose an opportunity to act. Feedback from this conversation could inform a notice review, but one person's experience does not establish the needs of everyone. Use a culture brief to prepare questions and the person's account to understand this situation.

slides.title: Practice: a loud conversation
slides.text:
Practice: a loud conversation

A caller speaks loudly about a service delay. Staff begin to interpret the volume as hostility.

An unsupported label could change the response and travel into later records or decisions.

Consider what was said and the communication conditions. How would you describe the exchange without guessing intent?
slides.narration:
Take a moment to distinguish what was heard from the interpretation. Loudness might reflect a poor connection, hearing needs, stress, or something else. It does not by itself establish hostility. What would you ask, and what would you record?

A calm check of communication conditions can help. Record specific behavior and relevant words rather than an unsupported motive. If there is a concrete safety concern, use the appropriate process; questioning an interpretation does not require ignoring that concern. Labels can travel into later conversations and affect how carefully someone is heard. Internally, the same issue arises when tone influences a performance judgment. Evidence about the actual exchange provides a fairer basis for responding.

slides.title: Practice: an earlier complaint
slides.text:
Practice: an earlier complaint

A person previously raised a discrimination concern. Staff expect the next conversation to be difficult.

That expectation may narrow listening and become a label that follows the person through later contacts.

How could you acknowledge the concern while hearing the current question on its own evidence?
slides.narration:
An earlier concern can be relevant context without defining the person. If staff expect a difficult encounter, they may become guarded or overlook the question being asked now. The resulting account can then reinforce the original expectation. Consider an opening that would avoid that pattern.

Listen to the current concern, explain available next steps, and preserve appropriate reporting options. Describe what is said and what remains unknown. A workplace parallel appears when earlier feedback determines how every later contribution is interpreted. That can affect supervision, development, and retention if no one checks the evidence again. Respectful listening does not settle whether a discrimination claim is established; it keeps the conversation open and the formal responsibilities clear.

slides.title: Practice: an offer of support
slides.text:
Practice: an offer of support

A family declines an option and calls it “welfare.” Their meaning and the person’s own wishes remain unknown.

Pressure to accept may weaken trust; recording a group assumption can affect later offers.

How could you explore concerns, explain choices, and respect the person’s decision without predicting beliefs from identity?
slides.narration:
The word may carry experience or concern that staff do not yet understand. The family might be worried about privacy, independence, how the option works, or something else. The person receiving services may have a different view. What question would give them room to explain without pressure?

Ask whether they want to share their concerns and who the person wants involved. Offer understandable information about choices and limits. Acceptance of the service is not the only sign of a useful conversation; informed choice matters. A culture brief can suggest context to explore, but recording its generalizations as this family's beliefs may mislead later staff. Keep the person's account, observed decision, and unresolved questions separate.

slides.title: Continuing the learning
slides.text:
Continuing the learning

Choose one service or workplace routine and trace how it could affect voice, access, or opportunity.

Prepare with a brief, listen to the people affected, and consider a response within your responsibility.

Name what you would check afterward. One DSD connects this learning with accessibility, cultural humility, community engagement, and equity review.
slides.narration:
Choose one practice example from the course or a general routine that you can consider without disclosing private information. Identify what people do, what that action makes easier or harder, and what might follow if it is repeated. That connection helps you see why intercultural learning matters beyond a single conversation.

Then consider a useful next question or adjustment within your responsibility. A culture brief can help you prepare; people affected explain how the routine works in their experience. Ask what would show that the response helped and what remains unknown. If the same issue appears across situations, related One DSD accessibility, cultural humility, community engagement, and equity review resources can help you examine the wider process. Continue learning without assigning colleagues a developmental label.

audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Explain how cultural meaning influences an ordinary exchange without predicting a person from identity.
Separate what was observed from what was assumed and check another person’s meaning.
Choose a useful adjustment to a service conversation or workplace interaction.
Recognize when one familiar communication style has become the standard for everyone.
